original_value: 3D image segmentation plays an important role in biomedical image analysis. Many 2D and 3D deep learning models have achieved state-of-the-art segmentation performance on 3D biomedical image datasets. Yet, 2D and 3D models have their own strengths and weaknesses, and by unifying them together, one may be able to achieve more accurate results. In this paper, we propose a new ensemble learning framework for 3D biomedical image segmentation that combines the merits of 2D and 3D models. First, we develop a fully convolutional network based meta-learner to learn how to improve the results from 2D and 3D models (base-learners). Then, to minimize over-fitting for our sophisticated meta-learner, we devise a new training method that uses the results of the baselearners as multiple versions of “ground truths”. Furthermore, since our new meta-learner training scheme does not depend on manual annotation, it can utilize abundant unlabeled 3D image data to further improve the model. Extensive experiments on two public datasets (the HVSMR 2016 Challenge dataset and the mouse piriform cortex dataset) show that our approach is effective under fully-supervised, semisupervised, and transductive settings, and attains superior performance over state-of-the-art image segmentation methods.

result.paraphrase: 3D image segmentation is crucial in biomedical image analysis. Many 2D and 3D deep learning models have already achieved state-of-the-art performance on segmentation tasks for 3D biomedical image datasets. However, because 2D and 3D models each have distinct strengths and limitations, combining them may yield more accurate results. In this paper, we introduce a new ensemble learning framework for 3D biomedical image segmentation that leverages the advantages of both 2D and 3D models. We first build a fully convolutional network-based meta-learner to learn how to refine the outputs of 2D and 3D base learners. To reduce overfitting in this complex meta-learner, we propose a new training strategy that treats the base learners’ outputs as multiple forms of ground truth. In addition, because this meta-learner training scheme does not require manual annotation, it can exploit abundant unlabeled 3D image data to further enhance the model. Extensive experiments on two public datasets, the HVSMR 2016 Challenge dataset and the mouse piriform cortex dataset, demonstrate that our method is effective in fully supervised, semi-supervised, and transductive settings and outperforms state-of-the-art image segmentation methods.
